title: A Brain Metastasis in Search of Its Origin: Occult Primary Non-small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: El Yachioui H, BenSghier A, Berhili S et al.
abstract: We present a case of a 67-year-old man who presented with right-sided hemiparesis and headache and was found to have a solitary left temporoparietal cerebral lesion on MRI, initially favoring a primary brain tumor. Further workup was unremarkable and the patient underwent surgical resection of the cerebral lesion. Histopathology and immunohistochemistry favored a metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma, though imaging scans showed no primary lung lesion. Subsequent PET-CT demonstrated hypermetabolic mediastinal, hilar, and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, consistent with occult primary non-small cell lung cancer. The patient underwent stereotactic gamma knife radiotherapy to the resection bed, followed by systemic chemotherapy with cisplatin and vinorelbine. At the time of writing, two of three planned chemotherapy cycles had been completed, with radiological response assessment scheduled after completion of the treatment. This case adds to the limited literature on occult primary non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and supports early tissue diagnosis as key to appropriate management.

title: Single-center Transformational Study on Feasibility and Efficacy of Respiratory Motion Management Using Novel Position Fixation Device for Lung Cancer Patients Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy(2023 No.358 Project)
sponsor: Tianjin Medical University Cancer Institute and Hospital
interventions: Novel Respiratory Immobilization Device for Lung SBRT
summary: This single-center study evaluates a novel body position and breath-holding device for lung cancer patients receiving stereotactic body radiation therapy. We will enroll 50 patients with single peripheral non-small cell lung cancer, compare tumor movement and radiation dose distribution with and without the device, to test if the device is safe, feasible and can improve treatment accuracy.

title: USP14 promotes malignant pleural mesothelioma progression and suppresses autophagy by stabilizing the YAP1-TEAD4 axis.
authors: Bai Y, Liu M, Zhang S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM) is an aggressive malignancy with limited therapeutic options and poor prognosis. Deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs) modulate protein turnover and participate in tumor progression, yet the biological function of ubiquitin‑specific protease 14 (USP14) in MPM remains poorly defined.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We examined USP14 expression in public datasets and MPM cell lines. Lentiviral‑mediated short hairpin RNA (shRNA) was used to knock down USP14. Functional assays including colony‑formation, Transwell, flow cytometry, xenograft model, autophagic flux detection, co‑immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination and rescue overexpression experiments were performed to explore biological roles and molecular mechanisms of USP14 in MPM. In this study, USP14 was significantly up‑regulated in MPM cell lines. USP14 silencing inhibited cell proliferation, clonogenicity, migration and invasion, promoted apoptosis in vitro, and suppressed xenograft tumor growth. USP14 depletion induced autophagy activation. Mechanistically, USP14 bound to YAP1, removed its poly‑ubiquitin modification and stabilized YAP1 protein to sustain TEAD4 activation. Overexpression of YAP1 or TEAD4 reversed the malignant phenotypes and autophagy triggered by USP14 knockdown.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings identify USP14 as one of the major oncogenic DUBs that drives MPM progression through maintenance of YAP1-TEAD4 signaling while inhibiting autophagy. Targeting USP14 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for MPM.

title: Integrative molecular profiling of TAM receptors and STAT-SOCS signaling in thymic epithelial tumors.
authors: Oner DA
abstract: Thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) are rare, molecularly heterogeneous tumors with a complex immune microenvironment. How TAM receptor signaling interacts with STAT-SOCS-mediated immune regulation in TETs remains incompletely understood. The TAM receptor family and STAT-SOCS signaling were examined in relation to genomic alterations, gene expression, survival, and the immune microenvironment, using TCGA-THYM genomic, transcriptomic, and clinical data integrated with GTEx normal thymus expression profiles. Expression of TAM receptors (AXL, MERTK, TYRO3), their ligands (GAS6, PROS1), and the STAT1-SOCS1/SOCS3 axis was assessed using GEPIA2; survival associations were evaluated using GEPIA2 and patient-level TCGA-THYM data, and immune infiltration using TIMER2.0. Cell-type expression of TAM pathway genes was assessed using TET single-cell RNA-seq data, and protein-protein interactions using STRING. Genomic alterations affecting the TAM-STAT-SOCS axis were infrequent, comprising missense variants and copy-number amplifications. AXL, MERTK, PROS1, GAS6, STAT1, and SOCS1 showed higher expression in tumor tissues than in normal thymus. Higher MERTK expression was associated with poorer overall survival in the GEPIA2 analysis, although not significant in WHO-stratified and multivariable analyses. AXL, MERTK, and TYRO3 expression were inversely correlated with CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration, whereas GAS6, PROS1, STAT1, and SOCS3 were positively associated with neutrophil infiltration. MERTK expression was positively correlated with CD274, and single-cell analysis showed MERTK was most frequent in macrophage/monocyte populations. TAM-STAT-SOCS expression was associated with the TET immune landscape, with MERTK showing an initial association with overall survival and further associations with T-cell infiltration, CD274 expression, and cell-type-specific expression patterns.

title: Cross-lineage mesenchymal transition in mesothelioma.
authors: Wu L, de Perrot M
abstract: Mesothelioma is characterized by extreme cellular plasticity, profound stromal remodeling, and near-universal resistance to therapy. While epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) has long been implicated in disease progression, mesothelioma arises within a uniquely heterogeneous cellular ecosystem in which multiple non-epithelial lineages contribute to mesenchymal states. Here, we introduce cross-lineage mesenchymal transition (XMT) as a unifying framework describing the convergence of epithelial, mesothelial, endothelial, immune, hematopoietic, adipocytic, neural, and stem-like cells toward fibroblast-like, extracellular-matrix-producing phenotypes. Mesothelioma is presented as a conceptual framework for studying convergent mesenchymal programming and XMT-related processes, rather than as a definitively proven example of XMT. XMT is driven by shared signaling axes, including TGF-β, Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, hypoxia, and mechanotransduction pathways that erase lineage identity and reinforce mesenchymal programs. Recurrent mesothelioma-associated genomic alterations, particularly loss of BAP1 and CDKN2A, further potentiate XMT by reshaping chromatin accessibility, cell cycle control, metabolic state, and inflammatory signaling, thereby lowering barriers to lineage plasticity. Integrative bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses reveal that XMT-associated gene signatures correlate with stromal enrichment, immunosuppressive myeloid and regulatory T cell infiltration, and poor survival in patients with pleural mesothelioma. XMT underlies mesothelioma desmoplasia, immune evasion, and therapy resistance, and represents a tractable vulnerability for stromal, immune, and plasticity-directed therapeutic strategies. Framing mesothelioma through the lens of XMT provides a unifying biological rationale for stromal evolution and identifies actionable pathways-genetic, epigenetic, and microenvironmental mechanisms that may be targeted to overcome plasticity-driven disease progression. This review highlights specific therapeutic strategies, including stromal-targeted approaches aimed at TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling, immune-targeted approaches that address myeloid-driven immunosuppression and inflammatory signaling, and plasticity-directed strategies targeting EMT/stemness programs and cellular state transitions.

title: A rare presentation of metastatic thymic carcinoma mimicking pheochromocytoma and Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome: a case report.
authors: Peikfalak F, Alishvandi A, Rahimi M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Metastatic thymic carcinoma is a rare and aggressive malignancy that may present with atypical clinical and biochemical features, posing significant diagnostic challenges. We report the first documented case of metastatic thymic carcinoma mimicking both pheochromocytoma and Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 54-year-old man presented with neck pain, microscopic hematuria, bilateral adrenal masses, fluctuating hypertension, and borderline elevated plasma normetanephrine, raising suspicion for pheochromocytoma. Concurrent retinal abnormalities and cerebellar lesions suggested VHL syndrome. However, serial biochemical reassessment demonstrated normalization of catecholamine metabolites, while ophthalmologic evaluation reclassified the retinal findings as hypertensive retinopathy rather than retinal hemangioblastoma. Brain imaging showed features atypical for VHL-associated hemangioblastomas. ^68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT demonstrated no significant tracer uptake in the adrenal or cerebellar lesions but revealed increased somatostatin receptor expression in an anterior mediastinal mass with tracer-avid lymph node and skeletal metastases. Histopathological examination of an adrenal mass confirmed metastatic basaloid squamous thymic carcinoma (CK5/6-positive, p63-positive, synaptophysin-negative, chromogranin-negative), excluding a neuroendocrine origin.
CONCLUSION: This case highlights the remarkable ability of metastatic thymic carcinoma to mimic endocrine and hereditary syndromes, resulting in potential diagnostic pitfalls. A systematic diagnostic approach integrating serial biochemical testing, advanced functional imaging, comprehensive clinical reassessment, and histopathological confirmation is essential to establish the correct diagnosis. Metastatic thymic carcinoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of adrenal masses with syndromic features, even when the initial presentation strongly suggests pheochromocytoma or VHL syndrome.

title: Probable Seronegative Myasthenia Gravis With Initially Negative Diagnostic Testing: A Case Report.
authors: Rodrigues S, Dias F
abstract: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterized by fluctuating, fatigable weakness. Diagnosis can be particularly challenging when symptoms are initially non-specific and standard serological and neurophysiological investigations are unrevealing. We report the case of a 27-year-old woman who initially developed progressive fatigue and exercise intolerance, followed by fluctuating left eyelid ptosis that worsened with exertion and improved with rest. Initial laboratory testing and cranial imaging were unrevealing. Persistence and progression of ocular symptoms prompted neurological assessment, during which an ice-pack test produced clear improvement in ptosis. Anti-acetylcholine receptor, anti-muscle-specific kinase, and anti-low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4 antibodies were negative, thoracic imaging excluded thymoma, and single-fiber electromyography of the orbicularis oculi was normal, providing no objective electrophysiological confirmation of MG. A trial of pyridostigmine provided only limited symptomatic benefit. In the context of the characteristic fluctuating phenotype, positive bedside test, exclusion of relevant alternative diagnoses, and despite the absence of objective electrophysiological confirmation, a working diagnosis of probable seronegative MG (SNMG) was established, and immunosuppressive treatment was initiated. Over the following two years, symptoms generalized, with limb fatigability, difficulty climbing stairs, occasional dysphagia, and substantial functional limitation. This case highlights the diagnostic uncertainty inherent to suspected SNMG and the importance of longitudinal clinical assessment. Negative antibody and neurophysiological results should prompt careful reassessment and consideration of mimics rather than automatic exclusion or confirmation of MG. In primary care, recognizing true muscle fatigability, diurnal fluctuation, and evolving focal signs may facilitate timely specialist evaluation.

title: PIPAC practice in Spain: a national benchmark defining evidence-driven restraint and a three-phase hypothesis of PIPAC implementation.
authors: Segura-Sampedro JJ, Ortega-Pérez G, Cortés-Guiral D et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pressurized intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy (PIPAC) has expanded internationally, yet its role remains uncertain due to the lack of high-level evidence and heterogeneous clinical adoption. In this context, national benchmarking is relevant not only for technical standardization but also for governance and patient protection in predominantly palliative settings.
METHODS: We conducted a national, cross-sectional, web-based survey (51 items) among 43 GECOP-affiliated centers (December 2025-March 2026). A total of 32 valid center-level responses were analyzed. Results were summarized descriptively.
RESULTS: Most responding centers were tertiary-level hospitals (78.1%) and public institutions (87.5%), all with established HIPEC programs and extensive experience in peritoneal disease management (81.3% > 10 years). An active PIPAC program was reported by 11/32 centers (34.4%), while 21/32 (65.6%) were not currently performing PIPAC. Among the 14/21 non-adopting centers that provided a reason, the main barrier was insufficient or inconclusive evidence (9/14, 64.3%), followed by organizational and resource constraints and clinical or implementation-related concerns (both 5/14, 35.7%). Only 5/21 centers (23.8%) explicitly reported referral of selected patients to active centers. Among active centers, procedural aspects were highly standardized, including universal adoption of a two-trocar approach (100%), balloon trocars (100%), and systematic safety checklists (90.9%). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed in oncological management, including chemotherapy regimens, dosing strategies, and integration with systemic therapy. The most commonly used regimen was cisplatin-doxorubicin (81.8%), with additional use of oxaliplatin (45.5%), taxanes (18.2%), or mitomycin C (9.1%). Response assessment consistently included peritoneal biopsies and PRGS (100%), frequently combined with PCI (90.9%), but remained heterogeneous in sampling strategies and adjunctive methods. At least one severe complication (Clavien-Dindo ≥3) was reported by 3/11 active centers (27.3%), this represents a center-level report rather than a procedure-level complication rate.
CONCLUSIONS: Within Spanish specialized peritoneal oncology units, PIPAC is implemented in a moderate proportion of centers with insufficient or inconclusive evidence being the most frequently reported barrier among centers providing a reason for non-adoption. Its current use is predominantly palliative, with gastric and colorectal cancer and peritoneal mesothelioma being the most frequently reported indications. It is characterized by marked heterogeneity in indications, treatment strategies, and response evaluation. This variability likely reflects the underlying evidence gap. Rather than discouraging its use, these findings support the need for structured development through prospective clinical trials, centralized data collection, and governance within experienced multidisciplinary teams. These findings allow us to propose a three-phase hypothesis of PIPAC implementation, characterized by initial standardization, subsequent diversification, and current uncertainty-driven practice.

title: A biomimetic SPARC platform coupling adaptor recruitment and BRS-Lck condensation for enhanced NK/T cell combination therapy
summary: Immune cell engineering has proven to be a promising therapeutic strategy for cancers and autoimmune diseases. Compared to classical CAR therapies, engineered T cells with modified TCRs (such as STAR-T and TRuC-T) exhibit lower tonic signaling and higher persistence. Inspired by this, we developed novel Synthetic Parallel Antigen Receptor Complexes (SPARC) based on the NK cell receptor 1 (NCR1) and the TCR chain. These SPARCs can recognize target cells via engineered extracellular domains and transduce signals by recruiting endogenous adaptor proteins (CD3{zeta}/FcR{gamma}). In NK cells,SPARCs confer high antigen specificity against lymphoma and enables NK cells to specifically recognize and kill tumor cells. Mechanistically, the cytoplasmic domain of NCR1 forms condensates with Lck kinase through two conserved basic-rich sequences (BRS), thereby promoting receptor clustering and enhancing NK cell cytotoxicity. Our findings indicate that SPARCs can also be applied to other immune cells expressing CD3{zeta} and FcR{gamma}. Incorporation of costimulatory domains further improves the performance of SPARCs. Furthermore, combining SPARC-engineered T cells and NK cells showed superior efficacy compared to either cell type alone. This biomimetic design preserves low basal signaling, overcomes the recognition limitations of endogenous receptors, and provides a versatile platform for engineering other membrane complexes.

title: Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
summary: We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.
